tldr: In the constructed hidden-treatment benchmark, learning every benefit sign still leaves a treatment budget costly: entire-class regret has order \(\min\{1,(\sqrt n\eta^2)^{-1}\}\). Its exact critical limit is \(F(\lambda)=J_\lambda(b,b)\), with two explicitly identified maximizing calibration fibers and an exact two-point least-favorable prior. At the exact elbow \(\lambda_* = \kappa_*/c^2\), the scalar optimizer leaves its boundary: \(F(\lambda)=(b/2)\Phi(-3\lambda c^2/2)\) for \(0<\lambda\le\lambda_*\), and \(F(\lambda)\sim b y_*\Phi(-y_*)/(\lambda c^2)\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\), where \(y_*>0\) is the unique solution of \(\Phi(-y_*)=y_*\varphi(y_*)\) and \(\varphi(y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-y^2/2}\). Original-record selectors attain the benchmark risk without population calibration inputs. For any broader hidden-treatment budget-decision class containing this benchmark with the same sampling and loss on it, only the converse transfers: its minimax regret is at least \((1/32)\min\{1,(\sqrt n\eta^2)^{-1}\}\).
gap: Regular hidden-treatment inference controls inverses of separated measurement channels. Local treatment-choice asymptotics compare risks at a fixed reduced-form point with shrinking ambiguity. Neither supplies an entire-class risk comparison when the effect-channel products are consistently learned but magnitude uncertainty persists over a nonshrinking interval. Generic finite minimax algorithms also require a separate bound connecting their finite game to the continuous statistical decision problem.
fill: The core asks for the exact critical risk as a closed-fiber Gaussian game, a structural reduction to balanced proxy products, explicit continuum discretization errors, and one uniform original-record transfer certificate. The resulting benchmark is directly evaluable to a stated tolerance and is attained by a data-only randomized policy selector.
